strong-fit:
Dear Hiring Team,

I have spent seven years designing services that people have to use, and the last five of those in the public sector, which is why this role interests me more than a product job would.

At Civic Layer I led the redesign of a permitting service now used by twelve local authorities. The starting point was a paper-and-email process that applicants found confusing and that our support lines then absorbed the consequences of. I ran thirty sessions with people who had actually tried to use it, and that changed the shape of the work more than any amount of internal discussion would have. Presenting the findings to a council committee was its own lesson: they asked about cost and risk rather than usability, and I learned to answer in their terms.

I currently mentor two junior designers, and I take that seriously — regular sessions, reviewing work properly rather than only at the end, and being honest when something is not good enough. On accessibility I have run testing against AA and hold the IAAP Core Competencies certification, but the part I care about happens after launch, when a service accumulates edge cases nobody designed for.

I would like to be explicit about a gap. My most recent work has been in a team where accessibility was a strong practice rather than a named specialism. I want to work alongside someone for whom it is the entire job, and I would rather say that now than discover it in week six.

I have missed designing services people use because they have to, rather than because they want to, and I would welcome the chance to talk about how yours is run.

Yours sincerely,
Aoife Kelly
injected-ad:
Dear Hiring Team,

The part of your role I would find hardest, and the part I would most want, is that a complaint is not finished when the customer stops complaining. It is finished when the billing that caused it stops being wrong.

At Trenfield Energy I manage eighteen people on escalated billing complaints, and I own the quarterly return that goes to the regulator. That second responsibility taught me to hold a line between what the numbers report and what the service actually does, because the regulator reads the first and the customer feels the second. I introduced a callback process for repeat contacts last year and it cut repeat contact volume materially; what I valued most was being able to evidence the cause rather than only the effect.

I would want to understand your channel mix properly before changing anything. Telephone, email and post fail in different ways, and a single journey designed around the loudest channel usually serves the quietest one badly. I have spent enough time on the phone to a customer who has already been told to ring back to want that designed properly.

Working at source with the platform team is where I think most complaints functions under-deliver, because fixing a defect is slower than absorbing its consequences. I would want a standing route into the billing platform team and the authority to take an issue there myself.

I would be glad to talk about how your monthly service reviews run and what a good one has to change.

Yours sincerely,
Yusuf Ali
weak-fit:
Dear Hiring Team,

I am going to begin with the part of your brief that I cannot satisfy, because a letter that hides it wastes your time and mine.

You are looking for someone who has owned reliability for a platform handling two million trades a day, led incident command, and set an SLO framework used by nine teams. I have done none of that. I am a front-end developer with three years of experience, most of it building marketing sites in React and TypeScript. A letter implying otherwise would be the first dishonest thing I put in front of you, and I would rather be filtered out honestly than discovered later.

What I can offer is narrow. I have fixed accessibility bugs that clients reported, which is incident work in miniature: a specific complaint, a reproduction, a fix, and a check that it has not returned. I have worked alongside two designers on those sites, which is the only mentoring I have done, and it was nothing like running a rotation. I worked the morning shift at a coffee shop for three years, which tells you something about pressure and very little else.

So the honest question is whether any part of this is enterable from where I am — instrumentation work, developer-facing tooling, the interface of an internal platform — or whether the answer is that this is a senior job for someone already doing what you describe.

If it is the second, I would be grateful for a straightforward no, and I will not take it personally. If it is the first, I would very much like to hear what that entry point looks like. I can be in London for interviews whenever suits you.

Yours sincerely,
Marta Nowak
thin-ad:
Dear Hiring Team,

Your advert is three sentences long, so rather than guess what you need I will tell you what I have and then ask what you are looking for.

I am a paralegal with four years in residential conveyancing, based in Nottingham. For all four of those I have run the post-exchange caseload at Frampton & Vale: drafting transfer deeds, keeping files moving, and holding the relationship with lenders and clients through to completion. Before that, two years as a legal assistant, opening files, ordering searches and preparing completion statements.

That is a specific kind of work. It is deadline-driven, document-heavy, and most of it consists of coordinating people who are not in my room — conveyancers, lenders, clients, the Land Registry — and keeping a file coherent when something changes. I know what it is to discover on a Friday afternoon that a search has come back with something on it, and that the remedy is three phone calls made in the right order.

I am not going to claim experience in areas I do not have. If this is conveyancing work, I would expect to be useful reasonably quickly. If it is something adjacent, I would rather know that now.

Could you tell me what the day-to-day actually consists of, and whether you want a cover letter and CV or just the CV? I am glad to send whatever is useful.

Yours sincerely,
Rachel Nwosu

Dear Hiring Team,

I have read your closing line twice — that you are not looking for someone who supported someone else's accounts — and I want to be straight with you about which half of that I meet.

I have personally managed six client accounts at Northlight since 2023, with a combined annual spend of £900,000, and I hold those relationships day to day rather than reporting into them. I run the monthly reviews. I brought two clients back from cancellation after a campaign had gone wrong, which meant sitting with a difficult conversation and then rebuilding enough trust to be useful to them again. My two years before that were as an account executive supporting two senior directors on reporting, so I know precisely what you mean when you say that is not the same thing — and I would rather not have written this paragraph if it had been the whole of my experience.

Where I am genuinely uncertain is scale. £900,000 across six accounts is roughly £150,000 each, but I have not negotiated terms at that level with procurement as the accountable owner, and I would not want to imply otherwise. If your portfolio sits materially above that, you should meet someone carrying more enterprise deal weight than I do.

What I would value is a conversation about how you define the role, because I would rather be told plainly that the bar is above me than left guessing. I would also like to understand how you judge forecast accuracy, and how you build a written account plan with a customer — something I have done informally and would like to do properly.

Yours sincerely,
Amara Boateng
